transcript.content: Hello, welcome. I’m Dr. [Your Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

They sent me in from the station. I guess I was… doing something they thought was a problem. I kept moving the airway bags around in the bay into this pattern that felt right, and I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud over and over.

My lieutenant told me to stop, but I couldn’t really step away from it. It felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad somehow.
Can you tell me more about why moving the airway bags and repeating the dispatch numbers felt important? Did you believe something bad would happen if you didn’t do it?

Yeah. At the time it felt like the pattern had to be right. The airway bags weren’t just sitting wrong — it felt like they were supposed to be in a certain order, and the dispatch numbers had to be said out loud with it.

I did think something bad would happen if I stopped. Not like I could explain exactly what, but it felt like the whole bay would go bad, like everything would be off or unsafe if I broke the sequence. My lieutenant told me to stop, but I couldn’t step away from it.
When you felt like you had to keep arranging the airway bags and repeating the numbers, did you feel anxious or upset if you tried to stop yourself from doing it?

Yeah, I did feel upset when I tried to stop. It wasn’t like normal worry exactly, but I felt really tense, like I was doing something wrong by walking away.

I kept thinking the airway bags had to stay in that pattern, and the dispatch numbers had to keep being said out loud. When my lieutenant told me to stop, I just… couldn’t make myself step away, because it felt like if I broke the sequence the whole bay would go bad somehow.
Do these thoughts or actions feel like they’re something you want to do, or do they feel more like something you have to do even though they don’t feel like they’re quite part of who you are?

It felt more like I had to do it. I mean, I don’t normally want to stand there moving airway bags around and saying dispatch numbers out loud, but in that moment it felt necessary.

I knew the pattern was right, and if I stepped away when my lieutenant told me to, it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. So it didn’t really feel like a choice.
Have you ever felt like this before, where certain actions or thoughts felt like they had to be done in a specific way to prevent something bad from happening?

I don’t know if I’ve had it exactly like that before. The main thing I keep coming back to is what happened at the station.

I kept moving the airway bags into this pattern that felt right, and I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud. When my lieutenant told me to stop, I couldn’t really step away from it, because it felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad somehow.
Have you noticed these kinds of thoughts or behaviors affecting your life outside of that incident at the station, like taking up a lot of time or causing you distress even when you're not at work?

Yeah. It’s not just that one time anymore.

I can’t really work the ambulance now. Even when they put me on desk-duty stuff, like notes and equipment checks, I wasn’t keeping up right or it got unreliable, and they ended up taking me off the schedule.

And outside work, I’ve kind of pulled back from people. I don’t see friends much, and stuff at home doesn’t get handled like it used to. It’s been messing with a lot.
When you were arranging the airway bags and repeating the dispatch numbers, were you trying to get rid of or neutralize certain thoughts or feelings that were bothering you?

I don’t know if I’d say I was trying to get rid of a thought exactly.

It was more that the pattern felt right, and saying the dispatch numbers out loud felt like part of it. If I stopped or stepped away when my lieutenant told me to, it felt like the whole bay would go bad somehow. So I kept doing it because breaking the sequence felt wrong.
